To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Japanese children selectively taught an ignorant person over an equally competent but knowledgeable person, whereas German children selectively learned from a knowledgeable person over an equally capable but ignorant person.

Japanese children were more likely to choose an ignorant person to teach rather than a knowledgeable person and were less likely to choose a knowledgeable person to learn from rather than an ignorant person, whereas German children were more likely choose a knowledgeable person rather than an ignorant one to learn from and were less likely choose an ignorant person over knowledgeable one to teach.
Japanese and German children show cultural differences in selective learning and teaching.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how children selectively learn and teach in a cultural context.
the question of whether and how the development of selective learning and teaching varies across different cultures.
children’s selective learning abilities and selective teaching abilities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the selective teaching and learning abilities are not universal.
children in Japan are better at selective teaching and children in Germany are better at selective learning.
the cultural differences in selective learning and teaching are due to differences in the socialization practices and the cultural beliefs of the two societies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Japanese children tend to be selective learners, whereas German children are selective teachers.
Japanese culture promotes children’s selective teaching and German culture promotes children’s learning.
Japanese children are more sensitive than German children to the knowledge status of the person they teach or learn from.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cultural differences in the development of selective teaching and learning should be taken into account in future research on the development of social cognition.
cultural differences in selective learning and teaching are likely to be rooted in cultural differences in the socialization process.
the tendency for selective learning is more pronounced in cultures that value individualism, whereas the tendency for selective teaching is more pronounced in collectivist cultures.
